The electricity supply companies are not nationalised, but owned on a co-operative basis.

brief_context: Compared to Denmark regarding electricity prices.
brief_extract: In many cases each consumer becomes a shareholder and has the right to elect members to a committee which controls their interests. The price of electricity varies greatly from place to place, and, while it was difficult to compare with our prices, it would appear that electricity is cheaper to use in Britain. Electricity is used exclusively for many jobs of work on the farm such as drying the oats and barley, stock rearing, milking, deep freeze, and also in the modern farm kitchen.

brief_context: Region noted for its heather-clad hills by the author.
brief_extract: I have looked: listened: learned. I had expected to find a flat countryside, so that I was not prepared for the heather clad hills of North Jutland, nor for the undulating countryside with the red tiled white farmhouses tucked into the fields of late harvest, nor for the woodlands clad in the scarlets and yellows of autumn. Of course, there were crowds in the city and the same traffic problem of rush hour, but in the rural areas one was aware of the emptiness of the roads, and of the peace of a country which depends on the land for half its exports.

There were not many automatically controlled

brief_context: Country where Danish consultants often spend a training year.

Their training, however, has a much more prac-

for entry into a domestic science college is one
year's service with a private household. This year is
often spent with a family in England, and probably
explains why the English of many was so good. Visits
There are so many things to talk about: visits
to factories, dairies and farms, schools, domestic
science colleges and universities; the co-operative
system on which so many things in Denmark are
based; the opportunities for all to learn and to go
on learning throughout their lives—the latest age
of entry to a course for Home Economists at
Aarhus University was 55 years; the commercial
kitchens of hotels and airports, and many other
sights and experiences too numerous to mention.

to be employed by the newly formed North of

years, and the Government had given the Board
powers to supply electricity to the country lying
North of the rivers Clyde and Tay, and to build
dams and generating stations to make use of the
vast resources of water power. This was the
beginning of what was to be the biggest boost for
Scotland within living memory.

article_title: TWO SCHOOLGIRLS' VIEWS OF MICRO-WAVE COOKING
brief_extract:
TWO SCHOOLGIRLS' VIEWS OF MICRO-WAVE COOKING
Bristol Branch had a demonstration of the Thompson Tappan micro-wave cooker, which requires no pre-heat period and the cooking time is only a fraction of the normal. By the action of the micro-waves the food generates its own heat and cooks from the inside, thus the dishes keep cool and only the food gets hot.

brief_context: Location of the Portway Secondary School.
article_title: TWO SCHOOLGIRLS' VIEWS OF MICRO-WAVE COOKING
brief_extract:
A chicken was roasted in 15 minutes together with potatoes and peas. Khurshid Zamen and Joan Newman, pupils of the Portway Secondary School, affiliated to the branch and situated in the Avonmouth Dock area, gave these comments :
This cooker is ideal for the working housewife as it cuts cooking time to 1/20th of that of an ordinary oven. It is economical and little effort is needed to keep the oven clean.

AN Annual Report must necessarily be a fairly impersonal document since it has to record facts and figures and to make general statements covering the whole range of an organisation's activities. Our own Report for 1962 which is to be presented at our Annual Conference in London on Tuesday, April 30th, is no exception although we do try to give acknowledgment for all the corporate and individual help which we have received during the year and to enliven the pages with some photographs of personal activities. We cannot adequately describe or depict, however, the human effort behind the many achievements which are recorded and which have enabled us to claim that 1962 has been another year of progress for the E.A.W.

brief_context: Region where new E.A.W. branches were formed.
article_title: The Director reviews THE E.A.W. IN 1962
brief_extract: We cannot adequately describe or depict, however, the human effort behind the many achievements which are recorded and which have enabled us to claim that 1962 has been another year of progress for the E.A.W. Fourteen new branches were formed, including two right up in the furthermost tip of Scotland at Wick and Thurso, so that now we can truly claim that our influence extends from Land's End to John o' Groats. There was an overall increase of membership throughout the Association which is a tribute to the liveliness and enthusiasm of our branches and an indication of the great demand for electrical knowledge of the kind which we can provide.

brief_context: Location of factories and showrooms visited.
article_title: Meeting the User’s Needs in Denmark and Sweden
brief_extract:
Appliance factories in Denmark
Appliance manufacturing works were of great
interest; a most modern cooker factory in Jut-
land, Lauritz Knudsen, included an impressive
radiant boiling plate test installation. In their
Copenhagen factory the company manufacture
an automatic washing machine in co-operation
with a British firm. I went in one of the com-
pany’s private planes to the Danfoss factory in
the far south of Denmark; this is the largest
producer of refrigerator compressor units in
Europe, and all types of electrical controls for
domestic and commercial purposes are also
made.

brief_context: City described as being built on many islands.
article_title: Meeting the User’s Needs in Denmark and Sweden
brief_extract:
I went also to
a factory where lighting fittings are made, and
saw the finished products there and in the
Copenhagen showrooms. Protecting the Scandinavian consumer
The city of Stockholm, built on many islands
with connecting bridges, provides enchanting
glimpses of the many waterways dividing the
old city from the new. I visited the S.E.M.K.O.,
which like its Danish counterpart, D.E.M.K.O.,
is concerned in the testing of electrical equip-
ment and their components for safety in use.

brief_context: Used as a comparison for appliance patterns.
brief_extract:
"Dry" demonstrations are given in the
showroom itself; the well equipped demonstra-
tion theatre is used mainly for work with school
children. Appliance design
Appliances followed a similar pattern to those
in Copenhagen: smaller ovens than in Britain;
a preponderance of solid, "speedy" boiling
plates; and many split cookers, some free-
standing, obviating the need for building-in,
and often reasonably priced. I saw more fully- and semi-automatic wash-
ing machines here than in Copenhagen; recom-
mendations of test houses are reflected in their
design, in that most of them employ the
"tumble" washing action; many of these ma-
chines are loaded from the top, and most of
them have stainless steel drums.

brief_context: Reference to the placement of washing machines in homes.
brief_extract:
An interesting
feature of some of the continental automatic
machines is the adoption of a colour coding
indication of wash water temperature according
to fabric needs; this took the form of "traffic
light" colourings. The washing machine in
Sweden is usually kept in the bathroom; it is
considered unhygienic to drain wash water
down the same outlet as the kitchen sink. The refrigerator is considered to be very
much a part of daily life; available models vary
in capacity very much as in this country, and
deep freeze units are becoming more popular.

brief_context: Location where a Head of Sherborne held an award.
brief_extract: From the beginning of her work for the Association, Dame Caroline Haslett always emphasised this aspect of education, believing that electricity could be a real emancipator of women, so that they could be equipped to give greater service to the community, and that idea was always associated with the E.A.W. Miss Reader Harris spoke of the awards of the Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust, and she was proud that a former Head of Sherborne School was a holder of one such award at New Hall, Cambridge. brief_context: Refers to the United Kingdom's electrical standards and colour coding.
brief_extract:
Although I know that 100°C is boiling point, I do not know how to convert °C to °F. I have also heard that the flexibles of some imported equipment may be coloured differently from those in this country."

To convert °C to °F, multiply by 9/5 and add 32, e.g., the equivalent of 60°C = 60 x 9/5 = 108 + 32 = 140°F (hot washing temperature). Incidentally, to convert °F to °C, subtract 32, then multiply by 5/9, e.g., the equivalent of 104°F = 104 - 32 = 72 x 5/9 = 40°C (hand hot washing temperature).

What it means today

location_standardised: New York City, New York, United States
brief_context: City where Richard Kelly's home is located.
brief_extract:
WILCOCK, AMIEE, FIES
Director-General, British Lighting Council

NOT long ago when I was in America I had the pleasure of visiting the home of a remarkable man called Richard Kelly, who is one of the leading authorities in decorative lighting in that country. What interested me particularly was the way he had used lighting in his own home in New York. There he has some of everything—lights that can be moved about on tracks attached to the ceiling, illuminated alcoves, floodlit curtains which give the effect of bright sunlight or subdued starlight from hundreds of miniature lamps, whole walls washed with light and portable lamps with huge drum shades containing as many as eight separate bulbs, which he can control by a dimmer to give softest conversational light or really high intensity lighting for detailed seeing.

Each member owned and used a refrigerator, and each represented different family circumstances, from the young married woman with no children, carrying on with her full-time job and running her home, through various stages of family life, to the retired couple with the younger members of the family returning on occasional visits.

brief_context: Location of engineering works where Geoffrey was an apprentice.
article_title: Advertisement: Central Electricity Generating Board - Feature on Geoffrey Castleman
brief_extract: After removing the valves Geoffrey must meticulously remove every sign of "blue blush"—the high temperature "rust" which is a turbine valve's worst enemy. This kind of work calls for the skill at a lathe Geoffrey learned as an apprentice in a Derby engineering works, and used in the RAF during the war. He came to Castle Donington in 1955 when the plant was being installed.
